literal: Yan Feng; Xu Qian; Zhang Gun; Cui Xuanbo; Deng Yuan
idiomatic: Biographies of Yan Feng, Xu Qian, Zhang Gun, Cui Xuanbo, and Deng Yuan

literal: Yan Feng, styled Zizhang, was a man of Dai.
idiomatic: Yan Feng, whose style was Zizhang, came from Dai.

literal: He loved learning, mastered the classics and histories in breadth, and was skilled in yin-yang omens and weft-text prophecies.
idiomatic: A devoted scholar, he ranged widely through the classics and histories and was versed in yin-yang lore and prophetic weft-texts.

literal: Emperor Zhaocheng had long heard his name and sent men to welcome him with ceremony.
idiomatic: Emperor Zhaocheng, who had long known his reputation, sent envoys to receive him with full ritual honors.

literal: Feng would not accept the summons.
idiomatic: Feng refused to answer the call.

literal: Thereupon he ordered the armies to besiege Dai city and said to the townspeople: "If Yan Feng does not come, I shall slaughter you all.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng then had his forces surround Dai and told the inhabitants: "Unless Yan Feng comes, I will put every one of you to the sword.

literal: " The men of Dai were afraid and sent Feng forth.
idiomatic: " Terrified, the people of Dai sent Feng out to him.

literal: Zhaocheng spoke with him and was greatly pleased, treating him with the rites due a guest.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng talked with him at length, took great delight in him, and honored him as an honored guest.

literal: Later he was appointed Left Chief Clerk to the Prince of Dai and took part in deciding state affairs.
idiomatic: He was later made Left Chief Clerk to the Prince of Dai and joined in governing the realm.

literal: He also taught the classics to Emperor Xianming.
idiomatic: He also instructed Emperor Xianming in the classics.

literal: Fu Jian sent the envoy Niu Tian with tribute.
idiomatic: Fu Jian dispatched the envoy Niu Tian to present tribute.

literal: He ordered Feng to reply on his behalf.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng charged Feng to answer in his name.

literal: Jian asked Feng: "What sort of man is the Prince of Dai?
idiomatic: Fu Jian asked Feng: "What manner of ruler is the Prince of Dai?

literal: " Feng answered: "Broad and harmonious, benevolent and loving, lofty in strategy and far-reaching in design—a hero of his age, who ever harbors the will to swallow the realm.
idiomatic: " Feng replied: "Mild and humane, far-sighted in counsel—a champion of the hour who constantly dreams of uniting the world under his rule.

literal: " Jian said: "You northerners lack steel armor and sharp weapons; when the foe is weak you advance, when he is strong you flee at once—how could you annex and combine?
idiomatic: " Fu Jian said: "You northerners have no plate mail or keen blades; you press forward only against the weak and run when the strong appear—how could you ever conquer all?

literal: " Feng said: "Northerners are stalwart and fierce; mounted, each man bears three weapons and charges like the wind.
idiomatic: " Feng said: "The north breeds hard men; in the saddle each warrior carries three arms and flies across the plain.

literal: Our lord is heroic and outstanding; he has made the northern lands submit, commands a million bowstrings, and his orders run as one.
idiomatic: Our sovereign is brilliant and bold; the north obeys him, a million bowmen answer his call, and his word is law to every camp.

literal: The army knows none of the hardship of baggage trains or cooking fires; it moves light and strikes fast, taking supplies from the enemy.
idiomatic: His host marches without the drag of wagons or camp kitchens; light and swift, it lives off what it seizes from the foe.

literal: This is why the south grows weary and broken while the north wins again and again.
idiomatic: That is why the south wears itself down while the north wins battle after battle.

literal: " Jian said: "How many men and horses does that state truly have?
idiomatic: " Fu Jian asked: "How many fighting men and horses does Dai really field?

literal: " Feng said: "Bowmen number in the hundreds of thousands; horses, a million head.
idiomatic: " Feng answered: "Archers in the hundreds of thousands; horses by the million.

literal: " Jian said: "What you say of men may pass; speaking of so many horses is empty boasting.
idiomatic: " Fu Jian said: "Your count of men I can credit; a million horses is mere brag.

literal: " Feng said: "From East Mountain to West River the Yunzhong valley runs two hundred li; from North Mountain to South Mountain it is more than a hundred li. Every year in early autumn the horses gather in vast herds and nearly fill the river valley.
idiomatic: " Feng said: "East Mountain to West River along the Yunzhong is two hundred li; north to south, more than a hundred. Each early autumn the herds assemble until the valley is all but covered with horses.

literal: Judging from this, what your envoy reports still falls short of the truth.
idiomatic: Judge by that, and even your messenger's tale understates the case.

literal: " When Feng returned, Jian heaped gifts upon him.
idiomatic: " When Feng went home, Fu Jian loaded him with presents.

literal: When Zhaocheng died, Taizu was about to move to Chang'an.
idiomatic: After Zhaocheng's death, Taizu was preparing to relocate to Chang'an.

literal: Feng, because Taizu was young and weak, firmly petitioned Fu Jian, saying: "The Prince of Dai has just died; his ministers have scattered in rebellion; the orphan heir is still a child and no one stands to support him.
idiomatic: Seeing the heir still a child, Feng pressed Fu Jian: "The Prince of Dai is newly dead; his officers have fled or turned traitor; the grandson left behind is an infant with no one to raise him to the throne.

literal: The tribal grandee Liu Kuren is brave and wise; the Tiefu chieftain Weichen is crafty and changeable—neither may be trusted alone.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren of the separate tribes is bold and shrewd; the Tiefu leader Weichen is sly and shifting—neither should hold power alone.

literal: You should divide the tribes in two and let these two men command them.
idiomatic: Split the tribal following between them and set each to command his half.

literal: The two have long borne a deep feud; neither will dare strike first.
idiomatic: They have hated each other for years; neither will dare move before the other.

literal: This is a fine stratagem for guarding the frontier.
idiomatic: That is the soundest way to secure the border.

literal: Wait until the grandson has grown, then preserve the state and set him up—this would be Your Majesty's great grace to a fallen kingdom.
idiomatic: When the boy comes of age, restore the realm and enthrone him—Your Majesty would then show supreme mercy to a ruined house.

literal: " Jian followed this advice.
idiomatic: " Fu Jian took his counsel.

literal: Feng soon returned east.
idiomatic: Feng soon made his way back east.

literal: When Taizu took the throne, he served in succession as Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, and Acting Director of the Palace Secretariat, and was greatly honored.
idiomatic: After Taizu's accession he rose through Director of Personnel, Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, and Acting Director of the Secretariat, and was held in high esteem.

literal: In Taizong's reign he joined Cui Xuanbo, Feng Yi, Liang Yue, and others in lecturing on the classics and in deliberating court policy.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Taizong he sat with Cui Xuanbo, Feng Yi, Liang Yue, and others to expound the classics and debate affairs of state.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Shizu's reign, for old merit he was granted the title Marquis of Pingshu and made General Who Pacifies the Distance.
idiomatic: When Emperor Shizu began his reign, Feng received the marquisate of Pingshu and the rank General Who Pacifies the Distance for long service.

literal: He died in the first year of Shenlu.
idiomatic: He died in Shenlu year 1.

literal: His son Cai inherited.
idiomatic: His son Cai succeeded to the title.

literal: Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary; General Who Pacifies the Distance.
idiomatic: He held the posts of Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Pacifies the Distance.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in office.

literal: His son Yuansun inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yuansun took the succession.

literal: He reached the post of Administrator of Boling.
idiomatic: He rose to Administrator of Boling.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died without further office.

literal: His son Shizong inherited.
idiomatic: His son Shizong succeeded.

literal: Xu Qian, styled Yuansun, was a man of Dai.
idiomatic: Xu Qian, whose style was Yuansun, came from Dai.

literal: In youth he had literary talent and was skilled in astronomy, charts, and weft-text prophecy.
idiomatic: As a youth he showed literary gifts and mastered astronomy, star-charts, and prophetic weft-texts.

literal: At the founding of the state he brought his household to submit; Zhaocheng commended this and promoted him to Director of Gentlemen for the Prince of Dai, with charge also of written records.
idiomatic: When the state was founded he came in with his clan; Zhaocheng praised him, made him Director of Gentlemen to the Prince of Dai, and put him in charge of the archives.

literal: Together with Yan Feng he taught the classics to Emperor Xianming.
idiomatic: He and Yan Feng together instructed Emperor Xianming in the classics.

literal: On the campaign against Weichen he was rewarded with thirty households of bondsmen for merit.
idiomatic: On the expedition against Weichen he earned thirty households of retainers as a reward for service.

literal: After Zhaocheng died, Qian moved to Chang'an.
idiomatic: After Zhaocheng's death, Qian went to live at Chang'an.

literal: Fu Jian's younger cousin, the Duke of Xingtang, Luo, held Helong and invited Qian to his commandery.
idiomatic: Fu Jian's cousin Fu Luo, Duke of Xingtang, who governed Helong, asked Qian to join him there.

literal: Before long, citing his stepmother's age, he asked leave to return.
idiomatic: Soon, pleading his stepmother's advanced years, he sought leave to go home.

literal: At the beginning of Dengguo he returned to Taizu.
idiomatic: When Dengguo was proclaimed he came back to Taizu.

literal: Taizu was pleased and made him Right Major of Horse, and with Zhang Gun and others he helped lay the first foundations.
idiomatic: Taizu welcomed him, named him Right Major of Horse, and with Zhang Gun and others he helped build the new order.

literal: When Murong Bao came raiding, Taizu sent Qian to report the crisis to Yao Xing.
idiomatic: When Murong Bao invaded, Taizu dispatched Qian to tell Yao Xing of the peril.

literal: Xing sent the general Yang Fosong with troops to aid, but Fosong dragged his feet.
idiomatic: Yao Xing sent General Yang Fosong with an army, but Fosong moved slowly.

literal: Taizu ordered Qian to write a letter and send it to Fosong, saying: "To lean on Heaven's mandate in cutting off the doomed, to ride righteousness in striking the benighted—never has merit shone without its season, nor achievement stood without its hour.
idiomatic: Taizu had Qian draft a letter to Fosong: "To wield the Mandate against a house already failing, to strike in the name of justice against a blinded foe—no triumph ever shone outside its season, no deed ever stood outside its time.

literal: Murong is without the Way; he violates our borders; his troops are old and weary; Heaven's hour of his fall has come—therefore I send this mission and army, and surely look for swift arrival.
idiomatic: Murong Bao is lawless; he tramples our marches; his soldiers are spent; the day of his ruin is at hand—hence this embassy and this host, and I expect you without delay.

literal: General, you hold the charge of a border province and command troops fierce as bears and tigers; the matter meets its moment—now is the time.
idiomatic: You hold a frontier command and lead warriors fierce as bear and tiger; fortune offers itself—this is the hour.

literal: If you strike on this basis, the campaign need not be fought twice; merit for a thousand years may be raised in a single morning.
idiomatic: Strike now and the war need not be fought twice; glory to last a millennium can be won before noon.

literal: Then hold high council in Yunzhong, advance the army into the Three Weis, raise the cup and toast long life—is that not magnificent?
idiomatic: Then feast in Yunzhong, march into the Three Weis, lift the wine and toast long life—would that not be splendid?

literal: " Fosong thereupon marched day and night.
idiomatic: " Fosong doubled his pace and raced to the field.

literal: Taizu was greatly pleased and granted Qian the title Marquis Within the Passes.
idiomatic: Taizu was delighted and enfeoffed Qian as Marquis Within the Passes.

literal: He again sent Qian to ally with Fosong, saying: "Of old Tang of Yin swore at Mingtiao and Wu of Zhou at Heyang—they called on the spirits to make loyalty and faith shine forth. To cherish the humane and be good to neighbors is the ancient standard; they drank blood and cut the victim to seal lasting peace.
idiomatic: He sent Qian again to swear alliance with Fosong: "Tang of Yin bound himself at Mingtiao, King Wu of Zhou at Heyang—each invoked the spirits to witness faith. To love the humane and treat neighbors well is the ancient rule; blood was drunk and the victim cut to seal peace forever.

literal: Now that we have sworn, let words return to goodwill; let us share disaster and relieve distress, sharing joy and sorrow as one.
idiomatic: Now that we are allied, let us speak only friendship; share each other's calamity, ease each other's grief, and make our weal and woe one.

literal: Whoever breaks this pact, let the spirits destroy him.
idiomatic: Whoever breaks this oath, let the gods strike him dead.

literal: " When Bao was defeated, Fosong returned.
idiomatic: " When Bao fell, Fosong marched home.

literal: The next year Murong Chui came raiding again.
idiomatic: The following year Murong Chui invaded again.

literal: Taizu said to Qian: "The matter is urgent now; without you, who could again bring Yao's army? Go.
idiomatic: Taizu told Qian: "Affairs are desperate; only you could summon Yao's host again—set out at once.

literal: " Qian had not yet departed when Chui withdrew, and the mission was halted.
idiomatic: " Qian had not yet left when Chui retreated, and the errand was called off.

literal: When he heard that Chui had died, Qian submitted a memorial urging Taizu to take the imperial title.
idiomatic: Learning of Chui's death, Qian memorialized urging Taizu to ascend the throne.

literal: Taizu approved.
idiomatic: Taizu was pleased with the counsel.

literal: When Bing province was pacified, Qian was made Protector of Yangqu and granted the title Marquis of Pingshu and the rank General Who Pacifies the Distance.
idiomatic: After Bing was pacified he was named Protector of Yangqu, Marquis of Pingshu, and General Who Pacifies the Distance.

literal: He died in office in the first year of Huangshi, aged sixty-three.
idiomatic: He died in office in Huangshi year 1, at sixty-three.

literal: He was posthumously made General Who Pacifies the East, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left, Inspector of Youzhou, and Duke of Gaoyang, with the posthumous title Wen.
idiomatic: Posthumously he received General Who Pacifies the East, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left, Inspector of Youzhou, and Duke of Gaoyang, with the temple name Wen.

literal: His son Luoyang inherited.
idiomatic: His son Luoyang succeeded.

literal: On the campaign against Murong Bao he served as Champion Major.
idiomatic: On the campaign against Murong Bao he was Champion Major.

literal: Later he was made Magistrate of Qi.
idiomatic: He later became magistrate of Qi county.

literal: Taizong, recalling Qian's merit, made Luoyang Administrator of Yanmen.
idiomatic: Emperor Taizong, honoring Qian's service, appointed Luoyang Administrator of Yanmen.

literal: On Luoyang's family fields three stalks of auspicious grain grew, each with strange ridges and joined ears; Emperor Shizu was pleased.
idiomatic: Three stalks of lucky grain sprang on Luoyang's land, each with unusual furrows and fused ears; Emperor Shizu approved.

literal: His rank was raised to Duke of Beidi and he was made General Who Pacifies the South.
idiomatic: He was advanced to Duke of Beidi and General Who Pacifies the South.

literal: He went out as garrison commander of Minglei and, after eight years in post, died.
idiomatic: He served eight years as garrison commander of Minglei, then died.

literal: His posthumous title was Gong.
idiomatic: His posthumous name was Gong.

literal: His son Jisheng inherited the title, which was reduced to marquis.
idiomatic: His son Jisheng inherited, but the rank was lowered to marquis.

literal: He died in the first year of Huangxing.
idiomatic: He died in Huangxing year 1.

literal: Luoyang's younger brother Anguo was Administrator of Zhongshan.
idiomatic: Luoyang's brother Anguo became Administrator of Zhongshan.

literal: Anguo's younger brother Andu was Administrator of the two commanderies of Guangning and Cangshui.
idiomatic: Anguo's brother Andu governed Guangning and Cangshui.

literal: He was further made General Who Displays Might.
idiomatic: He was also made General Who Displays Might.

literal: He was granted the title Viscount of Dongguang.
idiomatic: He received the viscounty of Dongguang.

literal: He died at the beginning of Tian'an.
idiomatic: He died early in the Tian'an era.

literal: Posthumously he was made General Who Pacifies the Distance, Inspector of Jizhou, and Marquis of Dongguang, with the posthumous title Lie.
idiomatic: Posthumously he was General Who Pacifies the Distance, Inspector of Jizhou, and Marquis of Dongguang, temple name Lie.

literal: His son Baihu inherited.
idiomatic: His son Baihu succeeded.

literal: He was Attendant Censor-in-Ordinary.
idiomatic: He served as Attendant Censor-in-Ordinary.

literal: Later, for crime he was removed from office and stripped of his title.
idiomatic: Later, convicted of an offense, he was dismissed and deprived of his rank.

literal: Xu Qian, styled Yuansun, was a man of Dai.
idiomatic: Xu Qian, whose style was Yuansun, came from Dai.

literal: In youth he had literary talent and was skilled in astronomy, charts, and weft-text prophecy.
idiomatic: As a youth he showed literary gifts and mastered astronomy, star-charts, and prophetic weft-texts.

idiomatic: When the state was founded he came in with his clan; Zhaocheng praised him, made him Director of Gentlemen to the Prince of Dai, and put him in charge of the archives.

literal: Together with Yan Feng he taught the classics to Emperor Xianming.
idiomatic: He and Yan Feng together instructed Emperor Xianming in the classics.

literal: On the campaign against Weichen he was rewarded with thirty households of bondsmen for merit.
idiomatic: On the expedition against Weichen he earned thirty households of retainers as a reward for service.
